old: we always believed that Zeus loved you more
new: we used to say that Zeus loved you more
reason: Butler: "we used to say that Jove had loved you better"; "always believed" turns a thing the heroes said into a private conviction and adds "always".

Butler: "all huge and hugely" is about the size of the fallen body; "mighty in your might" keeps the doubling but turns size into strength. Any wording that keeps both the size and the doubling would do.

old: a great tambour frame—an embroidery frame—in her room
new: a great embroidery frame in her room
reason: Butler repeats this passage at Book 2 ¶5 and Book 19 ¶13 ("tambour frame"/"tambour-frame"). Both accepted Books render it "a great embroidery frame" with no gloss. The draft brings in a third form and a gloss that is not at first use, and adds two dashes Butler does not have.

old: ‘Sweethearts,’ she said, ‘Odysseus is indeed dead. Still, do not press me to marry again immediately. Wait—for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—until
new: ‘Sweethearts,’ she said, ‘Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again just yet—wait, for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—until
reason: Butler's wording here is the same as at Book 19 ¶13 ("Ulysses is indeed dead, still, do not press me to marry again immediately; wait—for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—till"). Accepted Books 2 and 19 fix it as "Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again just yet—wait, for…". The recurring speech should read the same all three times.

old: when the months were waning and many days had gone by
new: as the moons waned and many days went by
reason: Butler: "in the waning of moons and many days had been accomplished", which is the same as at Book 19 ¶13, rendered there "as the moons waned and many days went by". Months do not wane, so "months were waning" is also a slip to the ear.

old: Then he cleverly had his wife offer
new: Then he cunningly had his wife offer
reason: Butler: "he cunningly made his wife offer". Amphimedon is describing a trap, and "cleverly" softens it. "Cunningly" is current English (D29).

old: nor any of his sons nor the other servants
new: nor any of his sons nor the other bondservants
reason: Butler: "the other bondsmen". Accepted Book 4 ¶54 and Book 7 ¶18 render Butler's "bondsmen" as "bondservants", and plain "servants" loses the unfree status.
Butler: "whose bondman are you". The question comes just after "nothing of the slave about them", so the unfree status is the point, and the Book 4/7 rendering is "bondservant".

old: my unhappy son, if he ever existed?
new: my unhappy son, if ever there was one?
reason: Butler: "my unhappy son, as ever was?", an intensifier. "If he ever existed" tells a listener that Laertes doubts his son ever lived, which Butler does not say.

old: his son was amazed to see him
new: his son was surprised to see him
reason: Butler: "his son was surprised". "Amazed" is kept from the live text and intensifies Butler's word.

old: attacking the suitors, and they fell thick on one another
new: attacking the suitors, at which they fell thick on one another
reason: Butler: "attacking the suitors whereon they fell thick on one another". The draft's "and" drops the consequence that "whereon" carries (GLOSSARY Book 4 row, finding 64.2). The draft applies that row at ¶0 but not here.

old: At this pale fear seized them
new: At this pale fear laid hold of them
reason: Butler writes "pale fear laid hold of them" here and "pale fear seized every one" at ¶43. The draft makes both "seized", which merges two of Butler's wordings into one, and "laid hold of" is current English.

old: So he spoke to them plainly and honestly, saying,
new: So he spoke to them plainly and in all honesty, and said:
reason: Butler: "so he spoke to them plainly and in all honesty, saying". This is the GLOSSARY Book 2 fixed formula "spoke to them plainly and in all honesty, and said:". It was first used of this same man, Halitherses, at B02 ¶8, and Books 7 and 16 keep it. "Plainly and honestly" breaks the formula.

new: best friend I have in the world
reason: Butler: "best friend I have in the world". This is plain modern English, and under D29 a repair restores Butler's own words rather than paraphrasing them.

Butler writes "the blue-eyed damsel". It is his only "blue-eyed" in the poem, and every other time he writes "grey-eyed". The draft silently harmonizes it to "gray-eyed" and does not record the change. ODY-RULES: reproduce Butler's facts even if they look wrong, and keep a difference he wrote (GLOSSARY Book 3 precedent).
